abstract: The proteasome is an essential cellular machine that degrades ubiquitinated substrate proteins to maintain proteostasis. Studies of purified proteasomes, however, cannot fully recapitulate its complexity. Here, we employ in-situ cross-linking mass spectrometry (XL-MS) combined with nuclear-cytoplasmic fractionation to characterize human 26S proteasome within intact cells. Our analysis reveals extensive compositional and conformational heterogeneity between subcellular compartments, along with distinct interactomes and dynamic states. Notably, we identify additional ubiquitin-associated proteasomal subunits and uncover compartment-specific ubiquitin-binding and ubiquitination patterns. Further we identify previously unreported proteasome-interacting proteins, including deubiquitinase USP15, and reveal a hybrid proteasome variant wherein translation initiation factor EIF3M substitutes for subunit Rpn9. Leveraging cross-linking-derived distance restraints, we model transient interactions and dynamic subcomplexes of the proteasome. Together, our work establishes a robust framework for in-situ structural analysis of large protein complexes and provides mechanistic insights into how compartment-specific architectures and interactions regulate proteasome function.

Methods
Reagents and materials
Tri (3-hydroxypropyl triazole) amine (THPTA) was purchased from TCI (Shanghai, China). Azide DADPS Biotin was purchased from Click Chemistry Tools (Scottsdale, AZ, USA). Cyanine5 azide was purchased from Confluore Biotechnology (Cat# BCA-32, Xi’an, China). Trypsin was purchased from Promega (Madison, WI, USA). High-potency streptavidin agarose beads and 1×PBS were purchased from Thermo Fisher Corporation (Waltham, MA, USA). 4’,6-Diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI) was purchased from Beyotime Biotechnology (Shanghai, China). Fetal bovine serum (10% dialyzed FBS) and streptomycin (10 mg/mL)/penicillin (10k μ/mL) for cell culture were purchased from Gibco, Thermo Fisher (San Jose, CA, USA).
In-situ cross-linking and subcellular fractionation
A stable HEK293 cell line expressing Rpn11 tagged with HTBH (biotin and dual 6xHis tag)
35
was used for proteasome extraction. Briefly, the plasmid pRK5/hRpn11-HTBH-IRES-EGFP was constructed and transfected into HEK293 cells using PEI. This plasmid allows for the co-expression of Rpn11-HTBH and EGFP, with the latter serving as a visual marker for transfection efficiency and normalization. Single-cell clones stably expressing the plasmid were isolated by limited dilution in 96-well plates. Incorporation of the plasmid was confirmed by PCR, and expression of Rpn11-HTBH was verified by Western blotting using a His-tag specific antibody.
293RPN11-HTBH cells were cultured in 15 cm dishes to ~90% confluency. After discarding the medium and washing with 1× PBS, cells were harvested by scraping, collected by centrifugation (500 ×
g
, 4 °C, 5 min), and washed three times with pre-cooled 1× PBS. Approximately 7 × 10
8
cells were collected, aliquoted into 1.5 mL microcentrifuge tubes (2 × 10
7
cells/tube), and resuspended in 1.2 mL of 5 mM BSP (in 1× PBS with 1% DMSO). Cross-linking with bis(succinimidyl) with propargyl tag (BSP)
34
was performed by end-over-end rotation at room temperature for 10 min, followed by centrifugation (600 ×
g
, 4 °C, 5 min) to collect the cross-linked cell pellets.
Nuclear and cytoplasmic fractions were separated using the Minute™ Cytoplasmic and Nuclear Fractionation Kit (Invent Biotechnologies, SC-003). Briefly, 1 mL of cytoplasmic extraction buffer was added per 100 μL of cell pellet volume. After vortexing for 15 s and incubating on ice for 5 min, samples were centrifuged (16,000 ×
g
, 4 °C, 5 min). The supernatant (cytoplasmic fraction) was collected, and the nuclear pellet was washed with 1× PBS and collected. All experiments were performed in triplicate.
Fluorescence imaging and Western blot analysis
293RPN11-HTBH cells were cultured on confocal dishes for 24 h. Two dishes each were assigned to experimental and control groups, with cross-linking performed only in the experimental group. All subsequent steps were carried out in the dark. The medium was aspirated, and cells were washed three times with 1× PBS. The experimental group was incubated with 1 mL of 5 mM BSP cross-linking reagent (in 1× PBS with 1% DMSO) for 10 min at room temperature. The BSP solution was then removed, and cells were washed three times with 1× PBS.
Cells were fixed with 10% formaldehyde (in 1× PBS) for 15 min at room temperature, followed by three washes with 1× PBS. Permeabilization was achieved with 0.2% Triton X-100 and 0.1% Tween-20 (in 1× PBS) for 20 min at room temperature, followed by three washes with 1× PBS. Click chemistry was performed by adding 1 μM azide-Cy5, 4 mM THPTA, CuSO
4
, and ascorbic acid (in 1× PBS) and incubating at room temperature for 3 h. The click solution was removed, and cells were washed three times with 1× PBS.
DAPI staining (1 μg/mL in 0.1% Triton X-100 and 1× PBS) was performed for 30 min at room temperature, followed by three washes with 1× PBS (10 min each). Cells were covered with 1 mL of 1× PBS and stored at 4 °C until confocal microscopy imaging. The fluorescence intensity of 120 cells was analyzed statistically.
Purification of cross-linked proteasome and enrichment of cross-linked peptides
Nuclear and cytoplasmic cross-linked samples were sonicated on ice (85 W) in 0.2% SDS (in 1× PBS) until clear. Pre-washed streptavidin agarose beads (20 μL per 1 × 10
7
cells) were added, and samples were incubated at 4 °C for 13 h with end-over-end rotation. Beads were collected by centrifugation (2000 ×
g
, 4 °C, 3 min), washed three times with 0.2% SDS, and proteasome fractions were eluted with 1.2 mL of 1% SDS (in 1× PBS) at 95 °C with shaking (1500 rpm, 10 min), followed by centrifugation.
Click chemistry was performed by adding 20 μL of 40 mM DADPS Biotin Azide (in DMSO) and 60 μL of click reagents (160 mM THPTA, 20 mM CuSO
4

g
, 3 min), and dissolved in 8 M urea (50 mM ammonium bicarbonate). Reduction (8 mM DTT, 1 h, room temperature) and alkylation (32 mM IAA, 30 min, dark) were followed by urea dilution to 1 M with 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate. Trypsin digestion (10 μg) was performed at 37 °C for 16 h.
Cross-linked peptides were enriched using 2 mL of pre-washed streptavidin agarose beads with end-over-end incubation at room temperature for 2 h. Beads were washed sequentially: three times with 1 M KCl (in 1× PBS), once with H
2

O (20 min incubation, 2000 ×

LC/MS analysis of cross-linked peptides

After column activation with mobile phase B and equilibration with mobile phase A, the sample was loaded, desalted, and eluted using a stepwise gradient, and the eluted fractions were lyophilized and reconstituted in 0.1% FA for mass spectrometry analysis.

Database search and peptide identification
For proteasome composition analysis, cross-linked peptides were identified using pLink 2 (version 2.3.11)
75
with a database comprising 33 proteasome proteins (Supplementary Table
1
). In addition, an
E
scherichia coli
proteome containing 2000 proteins was included as a background trap, alongside the built-in contaminant database built in pLink2 containing 293 proteins
76
. The search parameters encompassed a parent ion mass tolerance of 20 ppm, a fragment ion mass tolerance of 20 ppm, and a peptide length ranging from 5 to 60 amino acids. The cross-linker BSP was specified, targeting lysine residues and protein N-termini, with a mass shift of +376.211 Da for cross-links and +394.222 Da for mono-links. Fixed modifications included cysteine carbamidomethylation (+57.022 Da), while variable modifications included methionine oxidation (+15.995 Da) and N-terminal acetylation (+42.011 Da). Trypsin was designated as the protease, allowing for up to three missed cleavages. The results were first filtered by applying 1% FDR control for intra-protein and inter-protein cross-links, respectively, at the spectral level. Data from the three biological replicates were combined, and an FDR threshold of 5% at the PPI level for inter-protein cross-links and 3% at the site level for intra-protein cross-links was applied, upon aggregating matches at the spectral level. When estimating higher-level FDRs, we used the stringiest spectral matches without introducing higher-level controls, thus avoiding bias between target and decoy matches during data aggregation. The FDR values were calculated separately for intermolecular cross-links between proteasomal subunits, intramolecular cross-links, and mono-links, while preserving the original rankings for spectral matches. The computational procedures for FDR estimation are provided in Table
S3
. To further ensure the reliability of pLink2 assignment, we performed database searches using Kojak 2.1
77
and xiSEARCH
78
, which afforded >70% consistent inter- and intra-molecular cross-links within the proteasome, a level
on par
with the previous report
78
.
In the case of proteasome-interacting proteins, MS data were initially searched with pFind 3 (version 3.0.11)
79
for the identification of cross-linker modifications, utilizing the
Homo sapiens
database from UniProt (reviewed proteins only, downloaded on March 9, 2022). Search parameters included a parent ion mass tolerance of 20 ppm, a fragment ion mass tolerance of 20 ppm, and a peptide length between 6 and 100 amino acids. Setting a larger length range in the database searches allows the software to consider a wider array of possibilities without negatively impacting search accuracy, yet most identified peptides have lengths <40 residues. Fixed modifications included cysteine carbamidomethylation (+57.022 Da), while variable modifications encompassed methionine oxidation (+15.995 Da), N-terminal acetylation (+42.011 Da), and various BSP modifications (BSP-COOH +394.222 Da, BSP-NHS +491.238 Da, BSP-NH
2
+393.238 Da). Trypsin was set as the protease, permitting up to three missed cleavages. The FDR at the spectrum level was controlled to be less than 1%. The pFind searches identified fewer than 7000 proteins that were at least mono-linked with the BSP peptide, out of a total human proteome database of 23,700 proteins, thus keeping the dataset manageable for further analysis of cross-linked peptides. These <7000 identified proteins, combined with the 33 proteasomal proteins, were used for the large database search, which was subjected to the same stringent thresholds as the small database search for the proteasomal proteins. Following the separate database searches, we combined the search results and controlled the FDR with <5% at PPI level, as shown in Table
S3
.
The large database search also identified cross-links between proteasomal subunits, with results mostly consistent with those from the small database search. Peptide assignments differed in only a small percentage of cases (<3%), which could be attributed to: (1) homologous protein assignments, (2) non-homologous protein matches for proteins absent in the small database, including seven in the cytoplasm and four in the nucleus, or (3) poor spectral quality. We removed the ambiguous cross-linked peptides in category 2, which displayed similar fragment ions across both small and large database searches. This was done to increase the rigor of our analysis, as their inclusion would necessitate subjective expert evaluation or further experimental evidence. Together, we used intra-proteasomal cross-links from the small database search for structural analysis of the proteasome, and cross-links between the proteasome and interacting proteins were obtained from the large database search, thus to ensure methodological consistency. Since intra- and inter-proteasome cross-links do not overlap at the site/PPI level, this approach does not inflate the FDR values.
To determine whether protein identified with cross-links to Ub also have ubiquitin modifications—making the cross-linking intra-molecular—we also performed pFind3 searches for 19S subunits and proteins cross-linked to the proteasome, incorporating an additional variable modification—GG (dicarbamidomethyl) on lysine residues, corresponding to a +114.043 Da mass shift. Details about the modified proteins are uploaded as
Supplementary Data

Retention alignment and MS1 matching
To distinguish genuine biological differences from detection-limited observations in compartment-specific cross-links, we conducted an analysis based on XIC intensities. XIC intensities were extracted using pGlycoQuant
80
. For this, a precursor error tolerance of 10 ppm and an elution window of ±2 min were applied. pGlycoQuant considers M, M+1, and M+2 isotopic peaks, using a mass deviation threshold of 20 ppm for accurate peak extraction. A ResNet-based deep learning model within pGlycoQuant evaluated the quality of extracted chromatographic curves, enabling precise capture and quantification of true precursor ion signals by separating them from noise. Comparative intensity plots for nuclear and cytosolic fractions were generated, divided them into four quadrants based on XIC intensity distribution. An empirical detection limit, defined by a threshold from Quadrant I intensities (representing common peptides, Supplementary Fig.
3
), was used to differentiate truly unique cross-linked peptides from those potentially undetected due to lower abundance, despite generally higher intensities in the cytoplasmic fraction.
Our dataset comprised three biological replicates (BRs) for both nuclear and cytoplasmic samples. Within each BR, samples were subjected to small-scale reverse-phase chromatography, yielding six distinct fractions plus one unfractionated sample, totaling seven fractions for MS analysis, as described in the previous section. As varying liquid chromatography gradients were optimized per fraction, direct retention time comparison across all fractions was not feasible. Thus, we assessed retention time reproducibility for the same fraction across biological replicates (Supplementary Fig.
5

11

We selected commonly identified cross-linked peptides (those in Quadrant I), using the median retention time of their matched mass spectra as a representative value for alignment. For MS1 matching, the retention time window was determined by considering two factors: (1) Intra-experiment, intra-fraction retention time variation: The standard deviation of retention times for the same peptide within the same experiment and fraction was calculated. The majority of peptides showed an intra-group retention time standard deviation <2 min (mean = 0.383 min, median = 0.199 min). This robust alignment and stringent matching criteria ensure that any observed absence is indicative of a true biological absence (Supplementary Fig.

Construction and visualization of PPI network
Proteasome-interacting proteins and their extended interaction partners were constructed iteratively. Starting with pairwise cross-links, we progressively incorporated interacting proteins and their extended partners until no additional cross-links could be accounted for. All inferred interactions were cross-validated against BioGRID
81
(v4.4) and STRING-DB
82
(v11.5). Only experimentally reported interactions that could explain the observed cross-links were retained; all others were classified as novel PPIs.
When multiple protein assignments remained after filtering, nodes were collapsed into protein groups. Additionally, homologous proteins were merged into single nodes, with specific merging details provided in Extended Data. PPIs were visualized using pyvis (version 0.3.1): if at least one pair of proteins between two nodes was reported in BioGRID, they were connected by a solid line; otherwise, a dashed line was used.
Modeling and visualization of protein complex structures
Three complementary approaches were employed to generate pairwise proteasome complex structures. Initially, AlphaFold-Multimer
83
or AlphaFold 3 server
71
was used for structure prediction, and the resulting models were assessed and selected based on predicted alignment error. In cases where the initial prediction contradicted experimental cross-linking data, i.e., the predicted interface was away from cross-linked residues, predictions were repeated by restricting the modeling to the domain or segment encompassing the cross-linked sites.
Distance restraints were derived from cross-links between different peptides. Xplor-NIH
84
,
85
was utilized to incorporate intermolecular distance restraints derived from cross-linking data. Briefly, rigid-body docking was performed using the unbound structures of the interacting proteins, usually AlphaFold model for completeness. For each identified cross-link, a Cα-Cα distance restraint with an upper limit of 26 Å was applied, using a flat-bottom harmonic potential. A weak overall radius-of-gyration term was applied to prevent entropic expansion of the complex. For multi-domain proteins with flexible linkers, torsional freedom was allowed for linker residues with an additional database potential applied. In cases necessitating ensemble modeling with multiple conformers (Rpn13 interacting with Ub), the distance restraint was satisfied by the conformer yielding the shortest calculated distance
23
. The structures underwent refinement using simulated annealing, where the temperature was gradually decreased from 3000 K to 25 K. During this process, the force constants for the distance was for the distance restraints were ramped up from 2 to 30 kcal/mol•Å
-2
.
Additionally, we utilized generalized restraints assisted structure predictor
72
(installed locally) to model the structures of the Rpt ring and entire lid region of the regulatory particle (RP), both of which contain multiple subunits. The modeling was supplemented with intermolecular cross-links, applying a distance upper limit of 26 Å. We also employed the Chai-1 server
73
to calculate binary protein complexes, incorporating cross-linking distance restraints.
Validation of previously unknown interactions with the proteasome
HEK293 cells were seeded onto sterile glass coverslips in appropriate culture media and grown to 60–80% confluency. Cells were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde in PBS for 15 min at room temperature. Following fixation, cells were permeabilized with 0.3% Triton X-100 in PBS for 10 min at room temperature. To block non-specific binding, cells were incubated in blocking solution (5% goat serum in PBS) for 30 min at room temperature. For co-immunostaining, cells were incubated with primary antibodies diluted in blocking solution overnight at 4 °C, with the combinatorial use of EIF3M (Proteintech, 11423-1-AP, 1:100) and Rps5 (Santa Cruz, sc-390935, 1:200); EIF3M (Proteintech, 11423-1-AP, 1:100) and Rpn11 (Santa Cruz, sc-100464, 1:100)l; RPS5 (Proteintech, 16964-1-AP, 1:200) and Rpn11 (Santa Cruz, sc-100464, 1:100) antibodies.
Following primary antibody incubation, coverslips were washed three times for 5 min each with PBS. Cells were then incubated with secondary antibodies, Alexa Fluor 488 anti-rabbit IgG and Alexa Fluor 594 anti-mouse IgG (Jackson, both diluted by 1:200) in blocking solution for 2 h at room temperature in the dark. Nuclei were counterstained with DAPI (1 μg/mL in PBS) for 5 min, followed by three 5-min washes with PBS. Coverslips were mounted using a suitable mounting medium (ProLong Gold Antifade Reagent).
Images were acquired using a Leica STELLARIS 8 confocal microscope equipped with a 63× oil immersion objective. Representative images were captured to assess subcellular localization and protein expression. For quantitative analysis, cytoplasmic and nuclear regions of interest (ROIs) of equal size were manually selected using ImageJ software. Mean fluorescence intensity was measured within each ROI, and the cytoplasmic-to-nuclear fluorescence intensity ratio was calculated for multiple ROIs and cells. Statistical significance was determined using an unpaired
t
-test.
For co-immunoprecipitation, HEK293 cells were lysed on ice for 30 min in cold IP buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.4, 150 mM NaCl, 1% NP-40, 1 mM EDTA) supplemented with 1 mM PMSF and a protease inhibitor cocktail (specify the cocktail used). Cell lysates were centrifuged at 12,000 ×
g
for 15 min at 4 °C, and the supernatant was collected. Protein G magnetic beads (Thermo Fisher, 10004D) were washed according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The following antibodies were used: EIF3M (Proteintech, 11423-1-AP), RPS5 (Santa Cruz, sc-390935), and a control IgG antibody (Proteintech, 30000-0-AP, 1:200 dilution). Antibodies were pre-loaded to the washed Protein G magnetic beads in IP buffer for 1 h at 4 °C with gentle rotation.
The antibody-bead complexes were then added to the clarified cell lysates and incubated overnight at 4 °C with gentle rotation. Following incubation, the beads were washed three times with 1 mL of ice-cold IP buffer for 5 min each with gentle mixing. Bound proteins were eluted from the beads by adding 2× SDS sample buffer and heated to 95 °C for 5 min. Eluted proteins were separated by SDS-PAGE, transferred to a membrane, and were probed with antibodies against Rps5 and Rpn11.

Introduction
Maintaining proteostasis—the delicate balance between protein synthesis and degradation—is essential for cellular health and survival. The proteasome, a key player for proteostasis, selectively degrades damaged, misfolded, or unnecessary proteins, typically tagged with ubiquitin chains. Targeted protein turnover prevents the accumulation of potentially toxic protein aggregates, ensuring cellular homeostasis. Conversely, proteasome dysfunction has been implicated in a multitude of diseases, particularly neurodegenerative disorders, which are characterized by the buildup of misfolded proteins
1
,
2
.
The 26S proteasome, a 2.5 megadalton molecular machine, consists of two major components: the 20S core particle (CP) and the 19S regulatory particle (RP)
3
. The 20S CP is a barrel-shaped proteolytic chamber, formed by four stacked rings (α1-7/β1-7/β1-7/α1-7), which harbors catalytic sites for protein degradation. The 19S RP, which associates with either end of the CP, is responsible for recognizing, unfolding, and translocating ubiquitin-tagged substrates into the CP for degradation. Comprising 19 subunits, including the ATPase hexamer (Rpt1-6) and non-ATPase subunits (Rpn1-3, Rpn5-12, Rpn13, Rpn15), the RP is further organized into base and lid regions (Supplementary Table
1
).
High-resolution cryo-EM studies have provided structural snapshots of the human 26S proteasome in various functional states, capturing distinct stages including substrate recruitment, deubiquitination, translocation, and degradation of the substrate protein
4
–
10
. However, these in vitro structures mostly lack key components such as ubiquitin, intrinsic ubiquitin receptor Rpn13, and other auxiliary, transiently associated proteins and enzymes. Furthermore, nuclear proteasomes, which specialize in processes such as transcriptional regulation, cell cycle control, DNA repair, and chromatin remodeling, may exhibit distinct compositions and substrate preferences compared to their cytoplasmic counterparts
11
–
14
. Further adding to the heterogeneity, proteasomes can dynamically disassemble in response to cellular stresses
15
–
17
. Thus, the compositional and conformational diversity of the proteasome within its native cellular environment can be much greater than what has been visualized in vitro for purified proteasome complexes.
To investigate the compositional and structural landscape of the proteasome inside cells, we employed in-situ cross-linking mass spectrometry (XL-MS). XL-MS has emerged as a powerful tool in structural biology
18
–
20
, as it not only uncovers direct protein-protein interactions (PPIs) but also provides valuable pairwise distance restraints between the cross-linked residues, enabling data-assisted modeling of the structures of protein complexes
21
. Additionally, over-length cross-links, those that cannot be accounted for with a single conformation, provide insights into protein structural dynamics
22
,
23
.
While XL-MS has been used to investigate proteasomal structures and dynamics, those studies have been largely performed in vitro, focusing on purified yeast
24
–
28
or human proteasomes
29
–
32
. In-situ proteasome cross-linking studies are scarce, one of which identified 15 interacting proteins
33
. Here, we leverage an enrichable cross-linker developed in our lab
34
to expand the dataset of in-situ proteasome-centered cross-links. Our dataset enables us to construct structural models of proteasomal subunits and their interactions with other cellular proteins. Furthermore, by separating nuclear and cytoplasmic fractions, we have uncovered key differences in proteasomal composition, ubiquitination, and interaction. By streamlining in-situ cross-linking, high-resolution mass spectrometry, and advanced structural modeling, we have provided a comprehensive view of proteasome dynamics and heterogeneity within its native cellular environment.
Results
The workflow and quality control of cross-linking nuclear and cytoplasmic proteasomes
We used a cell-permeable, trifunctional cross-linker, bis(succinimidyl) with propargyl tag (BSP) to cross-link intracellular proteins
34
. BSP exhibited low toxicity to cells and diffused into the nucleus within minutes. After fixing the cross-linked cells, we introduced Cy5 dye through click reaction with the alkynyl group in the cross-linker (Fig.
1A

For proteasome and proteasome-interacting proteins, cross-link reproducibility was 78% in the cytoplasm and 60% in the nucleus. Furthermore, intra- and inter-subunit cross-links within the proteasome showed reproducibility of 80% and 63%, respectively. This high reproducibility can be attributed to our two-tiered enrichment process, which minimizes background noise from non-relevant proteins. Importantly, the variation between replicates within the same compartment (nucleus or cytoplasm) was consistently smaller than the variation between compartments, allowing us to obtain compartment-specific crosslinks.

The ATPase ring (Rpt1-6) forms a hexameric structure within the proteasomal base region and plays a key role in substrate unfolding and translocation
42
. To investigate its conformational dynamics, we modeled the coordinated movement of the Rpt hexameric ring based on intermolecular cross-links between subunits. Our calculations show that, in addition to the channel-closed state (Supplementary Fig.
14A
), a channel-open state is necessary to account for the observed intermolecular cross-links in the cytoplasm. Interestingly, the diameter of the Rpt hexameric ring in our model displays a more open conformation than previously observed in vitro, with the average diameter of the channel opening of ~14 Å (Fig.
3E

. This discrepancy can be attributed to a larger number of overlength cross-links observed for the subunits in base region of cytoplasmic proteasomes compared to nuclear proteasomes (Fig.
3A
). From a modeling perspective, to satisfy the pairwise distance restraints between neighboring subunits, the Rpt hexamer must undergo an iris-like movement, leading to a more open conformation. However, it is possible that some of the cross-links arise from transient states during Rpt ring assembly or disassembly

44

Discussion
Our in-situ cross-linking data have revealed a greater degree of proteasome structural dynamics and heterogeneity than previously observed in vitro, demonstrating the importance of analyzing large protein complexes in their native cellular context. The two-tiered enrichment protocol, along with the high effective protein concentrations within cells, allowed us to identify an extensive network of proteasome-centered crosslinks. These crosslinks captured diverse proteasome conformations and functional states within their native cellular environment, where allosteric regulation from Ub and other interacting proteins can further modulate their structural dynamics. Away from thermodynamic equilibrium, proteasomal functional states and structural dynamics should be very different from those characterized in vitro, warranting further in-situ characterization.
Our study implements rigorous quality control measures and therefore establishes a standard for identifying compartment-specific cross-links. By correlating precursor ion intensities and aligning chromatographic profiles, we have ensured that detected cross-linking differences reflect authentic biological variations, even given the lower abundance of nuclear proteasomes (approximately four times less than their cytosolic counterparts). This approach, in conjunction to comparison against known structures, allows us to confidently and precisely elucidate the structure, dynamics, and interactions of protein machineries in-situ. This methodology not only ensures the high reliability of our findings but also paves the way for future advancements in compartment-specific XL-MS workflows.
Proteasome is essential for maintaining proteostasis in the cell, and accordingly, it functions as a hub that is subjected to multiple layers of regulations. Through in-situ cross-linking, we identified previously unknown interacting proteins with the proteasome. By revealing cross-links to additional RP subunits our findings extend beyond the known Ub receptors Rpn1, Rpn10, and Rpn13. For example, Rpt5 has been previously detected through sodium dodecyl sulfate–polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE) and suggested as an auxiliary Ub receptor
7
,
66
, and Rpn10 has only been shown to interact with Ub through its UIM motifs.
Additionally, our study uncovered proteasomal interactions with PSMD9 and TXNL1, corroborating previous biochemical evidences
56
,
57
,
64
. Our findings also reveal an unexpected substitution of Rpn9 with EIF3M. Both EIF3M and Rpn9 contain PCI domains, named for their structural similarities among the proteasome cap (P), the COP9 signalosome (C), and eIF3 (I). Our findings, supported by structural modeling based on cross-links between EIF3M and Rpn5/Rpn8, two neighboring subunits in the proteasome, provide direct evidences for the existence of a translasome, a super-complex comprising both proteasome and ribosome
67
,
68
. However, structural modeling suggests that substituting Rpn9 with EIF3M within the proteasome would lead to substantial steric clashes, providing that EIF3M remains part of the 48S translation initiation complex
69
(Supplementary Fig.
19
). Thus, EIF3M-substituted proteasome is likely a distinct entity, potentially representing a previously unknown form of hybrid proteasome
70
.
Our study also presents a workflow for modeling protein complex structures in their native cellular environment. As intra-domain and intramolecular cross-links generally agree with the known structures, we could model the complex structure using rigid-body docking provided with sufficient intermolecular cross-links (>2). On the other hand, we found that AI prediction methods, such as AlphaFold
71
, often fail to generate structures that account for the experimental cross-links, suggesting the presence of uncharted or highly dynamic interactions. Nonetheless, cross-linking restraints can be used to rank the predictions and to confine the predictions to specific domains or segments. Additionally, sparse cross-links can be incorporated into AI-based structural prediction programs
72
,
73
, biasing prediction outcomes.
The limitations of in-situ cross-linking are also evident due to the sparsity of these cross-links, precluding high-resolution structural characterization. To enhance depth and to facilitate the differentiation between alternative conformational states, strategies such as enriching more cross-linked peptides, employing alternative cross-linker chemistries (e.g., photo-cross-linkers
74
), and utilizing orthogonal enrichment strategies can be further employed. Overall, our findings illustrate the power of in-situ cross-linking mass spectrometry in uncovering the compositional heterogeneity and structural landscape of large protein complexes within their native cellular environment.

Database search and peptide identification
For proteasome composition analysis, cross-linked peptides were identified using pLink 2 (version 2.3.11)
75
with a database comprising 33 proteasome proteins (Supplementary Table
1
). In addition, an
E
scherichia coli
proteome containing 2000 proteins was included as a background trap, alongside the built-in contaminant database built in pLink2 containing 293 proteins
76
. The search parameters encompassed a parent ion mass tolerance of 20 ppm, a fragment ion mass tolerance of 20 ppm, and a peptide length ranging from 5 to 60 amino acids. The cross-linker BSP was specified, targeting lysine residues and protein N-termini, with a mass shift of +376.211 Da for cross-links and +394.222 Da for mono-links. Fixed modifications included cysteine carbamidomethylation (+57.022 Da), while variable modifications included methionine oxidation (+15.995 Da) and N-terminal acetylation (+42.011 Da). Trypsin was designated as the protease, allowing for up to three missed cleavages. The results were first filtered by applying 1% FDR control for intra-protein and inter-protein cross-links, respectively, at the spectral level. Data from the three biological replicates were combined, and an FDR threshold of 5% at the PPI level for inter-protein cross-links and 3% at the site level for intra-protein cross-links was applied, upon aggregating matches at the spectral level. When estimating higher-level FDRs, we used the stringiest spectral matches without introducing higher-level controls, thus avoiding bias between target and decoy matches during data aggregation. The FDR values were calculated separately for intermolecular cross-links between proteasomal subunits, intramolecular cross-links, and mono-links, while preserving the original rankings for spectral matches. The computational procedures for FDR estimation are provided in Table
S3
. To further ensure the reliability of pLink2 assignment, we performed database searches using Kojak 2.1
77
and xiSEARCH
78
, which afforded >70% consistent inter- and intra-molecular cross-links within the proteasome, a level
on par
with the previous report
78
.
In the case of proteasome-interacting proteins, MS data were initially searched with pFind 3 (version 3.0.11)
79
for the identification of cross-linker modifications, utilizing the
Homo sapiens
database from UniProt (reviewed proteins only, downloaded on March 9, 2022). Search parameters included a parent ion mass tolerance of 20 ppm, a fragment ion mass tolerance of 20 ppm, and a peptide length between 6 and 100 amino acids. Setting a larger length range in the database searches allows the software to consider a wider array of possibilities without negatively impacting search accuracy, yet most identified peptides have lengths <40 residues. Fixed modifications included cysteine carbamidomethylation (+57.022 Da), while variable modifications encompassed methionine oxidation (+15.995 Da), N-terminal acetylation (+42.011 Da), and various BSP modifications (BSP-COOH +394.222 Da, BSP-NHS +491.238 Da, BSP-NH
2
+393.238 Da). Trypsin was set as the protease, permitting up to three missed cleavages. The FDR at the spectrum level was controlled to be less than 1%. The pFind searches identified fewer than 7000 proteins that were at least mono-linked with the BSP peptide, out of a total human proteome database of 23,700 proteins, thus keeping the dataset manageable for further analysis of cross-linked peptides. These <7000 identified proteins, combined with the 33 proteasomal proteins, were used for the large database search, which was subjected to the same stringent thresholds as the small database search for the proteasomal proteins. Following the separate database searches, we combined the search results and controlled the FDR with <5% at PPI level, as shown in Table
S3
.
The large database search also identified cross-links between proteasomal subunits, with results mostly consistent with those from the small database search. Peptide assignments differed in only a small percentage of cases (<3%), which could be attributed to: (1) homologous protein assignments, (2) non-homologous protein matches for proteins absent in the small database, including seven in the cytoplasm and four in the nucleus, or (3) poor spectral quality. We removed the ambiguous cross-linked peptides in category 2, which displayed similar fragment ions across both small and large database searches. This was done to increase the rigor of our analysis, as their inclusion would necessitate subjective expert evaluation or further experimental evidence. Together, we used intra-proteasomal cross-links from the small database search for structural analysis of the proteasome, and cross-links between the proteasome and interacting proteins were obtained from the large database search, thus to ensure methodological consistency. Since intra- and inter-proteasome cross-links do not overlap at the site/PPI level, this approach does not inflate the FDR values.

Retention alignment and MS1 matching
To distinguish genuine biological differences from detection-limited observations in compartment-specific cross-links, we conducted an analysis based on XIC intensities. XIC intensities were extracted using pGlycoQuant
80
. For this, a precursor error tolerance of 10 ppm and an elution window of ±2 min were applied. pGlycoQuant considers M, M+1, and M+2 isotopic peaks, using a mass deviation threshold of 20 ppm for accurate peak extraction. A ResNet-based deep learning model within pGlycoQuant evaluated the quality of extracted chromatographic curves, enabling precise capture and quantification of true precursor ion signals by separating them from noise. Comparative intensity plots for nuclear and cytosolic fractions were generated, divided them into four quadrants based on XIC intensity distribution. An empirical detection limit, defined by a threshold from Quadrant I intensities (representing common peptides, Supplementary Fig.
3
), was used to differentiate truly unique cross-linked peptides from those potentially undetected due to lower abundance, despite generally higher intensities in the cytoplasmic fraction.
Our dataset comprised three biological replicates (BRs) for both nuclear and cytoplasmic samples. Construction and visualization of PPI network
Proteasome-interacting proteins and their extended interaction partners were constructed iteratively. Starting with pairwise cross-links, we progressively incorporated interacting proteins and their extended partners until no additional cross-links could be accounted for. All inferred interactions were cross-validated against BioGRID
81
(v4.4) and STRING-DB
82
(v11.5). Only experimentally reported interactions that could explain the observed cross-links were retained; all others were classified as novel PPIs.
When multiple protein assignments remained after filtering, nodes were collapsed into protein groups. Additionally, homologous proteins were merged into single nodes, with specific merging details provided in Extended Data. PPIs were visualized using pyvis (version 0.3.1): if at least one pair of proteins between two nodes was reported in BioGRID, they were connected by a solid line; otherwise, a dashed line was used.
Modeling and visualization of protein complex structures
Three complementary approaches were employed to generate pairwise proteasome complex structures. Initially, AlphaFold-Multimer
83
or AlphaFold 3 server
71
was used for structure prediction, and the resulting models were assessed and selected based on predicted alignment error. In cases where the initial prediction contradicted experimental cross-linking data, i.e., the predicted interface was away from cross-linked residues, predictions were repeated by restricting the modeling to the domain or segment encompassing the cross-linked sites.
Distance restraints were derived from cross-links between different peptides. Xplor-NIH
84
,
85
was utilized to incorporate intermolecular distance restraints derived from cross-linking data. Briefly, rigid-body docking was performed using the unbound structures of the interacting proteins, usually AlphaFold model for completeness. For each identified cross-link, a Cα-Cα distance restraint with an upper limit of 26 Å was applied, using a flat-bottom harmonic potential. A weak overall radius-of-gyration term was applied to prevent entropic expansion of the complex. For multi-domain proteins with flexible linkers, torsional freedom was allowed for linker residues with an additional database potential applied. In cases necessitating ensemble modeling with multiple conformers (Rpn13 interacting with Ub), the distance restraint was satisfied by the conformer yielding the shortest calculated distance
23
. The structures underwent refinement using simulated annealing, where the temperature was gradually decreased from 3000 K to 25 K. During this process, the force constants for the distance was for the distance restraints were ramped up from 2 to 30 kcal/mol•Å
-2
.
Additionally, we utilized generalized restraints assisted structure predictor
72
(installed locally) to model the structures of the Rpt ring and entire lid region of the regulatory particle (RP), both of which contain multiple subunits. The modeling was supplemented with intermolecular cross-links, applying a distance upper limit of 26 Å. We also employed the Chai-1 server
73
to calculate binary protein complexes, incorporating cross-linking distance restraints.
Validation of previously unknown interactions with the proteasome
HEK293 cells were seeded onto sterile glass coverslips in appropriate culture media and grown to 60–80% confluency. Cells were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde in PBS for 15 min at room temperature. Following fixation, cells were permeabilized with 0.3% Triton X-100 in PBS for 10 min at room temperature. To block non-specific binding, cells were incubated in blocking solution (5% goat serum in PBS) for 30 min at room temperature. For co-immunostaining, cells were incubated with primary antibodies diluted in blocking solution overnight at 4 °C, with the combinatorial use of EIF3M (Proteintech, 11423-1-AP, 1:100) and Rps5 (Santa Cruz, sc-390935, 1:200); EIF3M (Proteintech, 11423-1-AP, 1:100) and Rpn11 (Santa Cruz, sc-100464, 1:100)l; RPS5 (Proteintech, 16964-1-AP, 1:200) and Rpn11 (Santa Cruz, sc-100464, 1:100) antibodies.
Following primary antibody incubation, coverslips were washed three times for 5 min each with PBS. Cells were then incubated with secondary antibodies, Alexa Fluor 488 anti-rabbit IgG and Alexa Fluor 594 anti-mouse IgG (Jackson, both diluted by 1:200) in blocking solution for 2 h at room temperature in the dark. Nuclei were counterstained with DAPI (1 μg/mL in PBS) for 5 min, followed by three 5-min washes with PBS. Coverslips were mounted using a suitable mounting medium (ProLong Gold Antifade Reagent).
Images were acquired using a Leica STELLARIS 8 confocal microscope equipped with a 63× oil immersion objective. Representative images were captured to assess subcellular localization and protein expression. Mean fluorescence intensity was measured within each ROI, and the cytoplasmic-to-nuclear fluorescence intensity ratio was calculated for multiple ROIs and cells. Statistical significance was determined using an unpaired
t
-test.

g
for 15 min at 4 °C, and the supernatant was collected. Protein G magnetic beads (Thermo Fisher, 10004D) were washed according to the manufacturer’s instructions.
